title: Memento: Fine-tuning LLM Agents without Fine-tuning LLMs
authors: Huichi Zhou, Yihang Chen, Siyuan Guo, et al.
mechanism: State: a Case Bank of (state, action, reward) tuples; state is encoded by a frozen text encoder (SimCSE), action and reward kept in original form. Planner-executor loop: the planner LLM (GPT-4.1) retrieves K cases, plans, the executor (o3 / o4-mini) calls tools over MCP; the case is written only on task completion (final step of each trajectory). Write appends (s,a,r) (non-parametric), or additionally updates a Q-function online (parametric). Read is cosine-similarity top-K over SimCSE embeddings (non-parametric) or top-K by a learned Q(s,c;theta) two-layer MLP (parametric). No verification gate on writes: the reward label (success/fail) is the only filter; both successes and failures are stored.
evidence: GAIA validation 87.88% Pass@3 (top-1), GAIA test 79.40%; DeepResearcher 66.6% F1 and 80.4% PM; case-based memory adds 4.7 to 9.6 absolute points on out-of-distribution tasks (abstract). HLE: 24.4% PM with planner GPT-4.1 / executor o4-mini, vs GPT-5 25.32%. Retrieval K: best at K=4 (F1 64.5, PM 78.5) on DeepResearcher.
cost: Sec 6.1 samples 10 GAIA validation tasks: Level 1 26k input / 4.7k output tokens, Level 2 48k/6.9k, Level 3 121k/9.8k per task. No dollar figure seen in the passages read.
verified: arXiv API record + arXiv HTML full text (read relevant sections)
could_not_verify: Dollar cost per task not looked for beyond the token table; Figure 6 values are from the text, not the figure. | repo redirects to https://github.com/Memento-Teams/Memento (main branch only; no Memento 2/3 folder).

title: Memento 2: Learning by Stateful Reflective Memory
authors: Jun Wang
mechanism: Theory paper (35 pp, no new experiments seen; it cites earlier empirical work [Memento, CBR LLMs]). Defines a Stateful Reflective Decision Process: augmented state x=(s, M) with episodic memory M; Write(M,s,a,r,s') is policy evaluation, Read via retrieval policy mu(c|s,M) is policy improvement; mu 'may be similarity-based or learned'. Instantiated as soft policy iteration with a convergence guarantee as memory covers the state space. No acceptance gate on writes is defined beyond the reward.
evidence: No benchmark numbers of its own. States convergence of the composite policy to optimal as memory expands (theorem).
cost: not stated
verified: arXiv API record + arXiv HTML full text (read relevant sections)
could_not_verify: Searched for experiments, benchmarks, accuracy, code link: none found. Section 'Experimental support, please' appears as a stray line (line ~1898) i.e. a placeholder.

title: Memento-Skills: Let Agents Design Agents
authors: Huichi Zhou, Siyuan Guo, Anjie Liu, et al.
mechanism: State: a skill library; each skill is a folder with a declarative SKILL.md spec plus helper scripts and prompts, plus a 'tip memory' and per-skill running utility U = n_succ/(n_succ+n_fail). Read: a skill router (single-step offline-RL-trained embedding model, multi-positive InfoNCE on ~3k seed skills crawled from ~8k, memento-Qwen) picks a skill. After a failed attempt, an LLM failure-attribution selector picks the single responsible skill; a rewriter proposes file-level edits; if U < threshold delta (and n >= n_min) it instead discovers a new/restructured skill. Acceptance: 'all mutations are guarded by an automatic unit-test gate, a synthetic test case is generated, executed through the updated skill, and scored by the judge'; rollback on failure. Retry up to K rounds.
evidence: GAIA (100 train / 65 test from validation): training success 65.1% first attempt to 91.6% by third round; test 66.0% vs 52.3% Read-Write ablation (+13.7 pts). HLE (788 train / 342 test): training 30.8% (R0) to 54.5% (R3); test 38.7% vs 17.9% baseline. Library grows from 5 atomic skills to 41 (GAIA) and 235 (HLE).
cost: Backbone: Gemini-3.1-Flash for all experiments. No tokens or dollars per task seen.
verified: arXiv API record + arXiv HTML full text (read relevant sections)
could_not_verify: The gate's test is synthetic and judged by an LLM, not an external ground truth; no ablation of the gate alone found. No per-task cost.

title: ARC-AGI-3: A New Challenge for Frontier Agentic Intelligence
authors: ARC Prize Foundation
mechanism: Benchmark paper, not an agent. ARC-AGI-3 is an interactive benchmark of novel abstract turn-based environments (64x64 frame observations) where the agent must explore, infer goals, model dynamics and plan with no instructions, using Core Knowledge priors only. Each env has >=6 levels (scoring formula assumes n=5), built in an in-house Python engine and calibrated on 10 human testers per env (solved by >=2 independently). Score is RHAE: per level S=min(1.15, h/a)^2 with h = upper-median best first-run human action count, a = agent actions; environment score = level-index-weighted average (w_l=l) capped at the weighted fraction of levels completed; total = mean over environments. Evaluation runs with an action cap of 5x human median per level.
evidence: Dataset sizes (Table 1): Public Demo 25, Semi-Private 55, Fully Private 55 (sum 135). Humans solve 100% of environments; abstract: frontier AI 'as of March 2026, score below 1%'. Semi-private leaderboard at release (Table 2): Opus 4.6 (Max) 0.50%, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview 0.40%, GPT 5.4 (High) 0.20%, Grok-4.20 (Beta 0309 Reasoning) 0.10%. Human data: 486 participants, 414 candidate envs, 2,893 attempts, 427.9 hours, median attempt 7.4 min. Preview competition (3 public + 3 hidden envs, 30 days 2025): StochasticGoose 12.58% (1st), Blind Squirrel 6.71% (2nd). Harness effect: TR87 variant Opus 4.6 0.0% no harness vs 97.1% Duke harness; BP35 0.0% under both.
cost: Paper says full eval of high-reasoning frontier models costs 'tens of thousands of dollars in API costs', hence 5x-human-median action cap. Official leaderboard uses one system prompt, no harness, no tools. Humans paid $115-$140 per session plus $5 per solved env.
verified: arXiv API record + arXiv HTML full text (read relevant sections)
could_not_verify: Per-model dollar cost per run not stated (only 'tens of thousands of dollars'). Duke harness sentence on public-set results is truncated in the extracted text. Formula assumes n=5 levels while design rule says at least six levels per env; paper text not reconciled. | other repos cited: arcprize/ARC-AGI-Community-Leaderboard, symbolica-ai/ARC-AGI-3-Agents

title: Executable World Models for ARC-AGI-3 in the Era of Coding Agents
authors: Sergey Rodionov
mechanism: Baseline: a Codex CLI (v0.128.0) coding agent driven by a scripted external controller. The agent maintains a Python codebase as an executable world model (world_model_engine.py transitions, world_model_state_io.py state/rendering, world_model_main_planner.py planner, all starting as empty interface templates). A world-model verifier replays recorded observations; a planner verifier checks plans reach LEVEL_COMPLETED in the model; a plan executor simulates a plan in the model and runs it in the real game, stopping at the first predicted-vs-observed settled ASCII frame mismatch (treated as a blocking modeling error). Controller prompts repeated refactoring toward simpler abstractions as an MDL proxy, issues RESET on GAME_OVER, and restarts a stalled agent up to ten times. No game-specific code or prompts.
evidence: 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games, one fresh playthrough each. GPT-5.5 high reasoning: fully solved 15 games, mean per-game RHAE 58.12%. GPT-5.4 high reasoning: fully solved 8 games, mean per-game RHAE 41.29%. Variability: ft09 100.00% RHAE with GPT-5.4 vs 57.80% with GPT-5.5; wa30 49.77% (7/9 levels) vs 9.11% (4/9 levels) (which model is which on wa30: text says 'compared with ... GPT-5.5', so the 49.77% run is GPT-5.4).
cost: A single ChatGPT Pro subscription (USD 200 per month) was sufficient for roughly two to eight games per weekly Codex limit with GPT-5.5 high. No token counts or per-game dollars.
verified: arXiv API record + arXiv HTML full text (read relevant sections)
could_not_verify: Private validation / semi-private score not reported ('not yet available to us'). No token counts. Per-game cost only as subscription-limit scale. Earlier harness versions leaked game identity (web search, second game client as simulator); those results excluded from reported scores. Development mostly on public game ls20.

title: Do Coding Agents Need Executable World Models, Simplification, and Verification to Solve ARC-AGI-3?
authors: Sergey Rodionov
mechanism: Controlled ablation of Rodionov's earlier agent (Codex-based) with four variants: textual world model (twma), flexible-interface executable model (ewma), executable + scheduled simplification prompts (ewma_s), and fixed-interface executable + simplification + exact replay verification of past actions against recorded observations (ewma_sv). Each playthrough is a fresh agent process, one game, no carry-over. Verification = replay recorded actions in the model; predictions must match recorded observations exactly; mismatch is the signal for revision.
evidence: Mean RHAE over 25 public games (Table 2), textual / executable / simplification / verification: gpt-5.4 high 34.16/33.54/30.60/39.16; gpt-5.4 xhigh 40.67/44.72/53.10/53.72; gpt-5.5 high 58.85/51.16/58.35/65.64; gpt-5.5 xhigh 72.51/69.70/73.09/74.78. Follow-up gpt-5.6-sol: verification variant completes every public level at xhigh and max (98.97 and 98.77 RHAE, v1.6); textual completes all at max (95.97) with 41% fewer actions than human baseline.
cost: Cost tokens (weighted proxy, not dollars; 1M cost tokens = USD 15 for gpt-5.4, USD 30 for gpt-5.5), millions summed over 25 games, textual/exec/simpl/verif: 5.4 high 81.30/66.38/127.27/147.65; 5.5 xhigh 68.16/74.02/163.47/222.06. Verification uses 1.82-3.26x the textual variant's cost tokens. Runs used nine ChatGPT Pro subscriptions (USD 1,800 total); median wall clock 4h26m, mean 6h08m, max 53h08m per playthrough. Authors say API cost would be roughly 5x the cache-mix projection.
verified: arXiv API record + arXiv HTML full text (read relevant sections)
could_not_verify: No verification-without-simplification variant exists, so verification alone is untested (paper says so). Single run per game per cell; public set only, contamination not excluded. Abstract wording 'verification useful' is supported only as 'ranked first in all four settings, margin 0.62 to 8.56 points over simplification'.

title: OPINE-World: Programmatic World Modeling with Ontology-error-Prioritized Interactive Exploration for ARC-AGI-3
authors: David Courtis, Wenhao Li, Scott Sanner
mechanism: Hybrid world model kept per game: a qualitative object-oriented natural-language model (S_NL,T_NL,R_NL), a Bayesian belief state S_B of empirical object-type x action x context effect distributions built by a deterministic replay-based extractor, and executable Python transition/reward models plus planner and an observation-to-object abstraction. Every observation goes into a replay buffer D and updates S_B. Acceptance gate: the programmatic model must be replay-consistent (Phi_1): for all stored transitions, predicted successor fields and reward equal the observed ones. A mismatch stops the current plan, opens a short window collecting related counterexamples, and triggers synthesis repair (CEGIS-style). A consistent model plans toward reward (Phi_2: planned sequence reaches reward in the model, executed as an online test of the model); if no such plan exists, S_B posterior uncertainty directs epistemic experiments to find confounders. Only deterministic discrete envs are handled.
evidence: Claude Opus 4.8 high on 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games: RHAE 1.5% base to 78.40%; 20/25 games, 160/183 levels completed. Table 1 mean+-SE: Full 78.4+-6.3; No S_B 58.2+-8.3; baseline1 63.7+-7.4; DreamTeam 38.1+-7.6; Continual 20.5+-5.7; OpenClaw 5.2+-1.0 (games completed 20, 12, 14, 6, 3, 0 of 25). Removing S_B reduces RHAE by 20.24 points. Only system better on Community leaderboard as of July 25, 2026: NVIDIA NOOA on GPT-5.6-sol xhigh, 85.1%; paper notes a 4.6x RHAE gap between Opus 4.8 high and GPT 5.6 Sol xhigh base models. Per-game budget 2000 actions or stall of >500 actions per level.
cost: A complete 25-game evaluation uses Claude Opus 4.8 at high reasoning effort; including replay and planning, individual environments can consume up to 2 billion cumulative tokens. No dollar or wall-clock figure.
verified: arXiv API record + arXiv HTML full text (read relevant sections)
could_not_verify: No code URL (supplementary material only). No per-task dollar cost. Not stated whether Table 1 is a single run per game; RQ2/RQ3 ablations use low effort and a single case game g50t. baseline1 in Table 1 scores 63.7 here vs 58.12 reported in 2605.05138 because paper says it uses matching game builds and scoring; model behind baseline1 in this table not verified. Limitations: only deterministic discrete environments; replay consistency gives no guarantee for unvisited objects. Author-flagged negative: in some games (e.g. tr87) Bayesian guidance investigates goal-irrelevant uncertainty. | code note: Source code is 'provided as supplementary material'; no URL given in the text.

title: Tycho: Active Abstraction with Programmatic World Models for ARC-AGI-3
authors: Jens Lehmann, Andrei Aioanei, Sahar Vahdati
mechanism: Coding-agent system (Python) with typed durable evidence (decision frames separated from transient, terminal, fatal, reset frames; wmlib library; per-level files) and a free-form executable world model the agent may build, verify, plan with, repair or bypass. Verification replays the latest attempt per level from its first frame and compares predicted to recorded successors cell by cell (accuracy on claimed pixels plus coverage); outcomes (level_complete/game_over) verified separately. Planning searches the program for a route to level_complete and writes a validated, hash-anchored artifact that the actor treats as conditional advice. Four orchestration policies compared: no world model, single (actor-authored), orchestrator (actor-requested delegation to a builder), trigger (automatic builder call on verification failure).
evidence: Claude Opus 4.8, 25 public games, one run per policy (RHAE): no world model 79.07, single 85.36, orchestrator 88.49, trigger 83.07; games completed 19/19/21/18, levels 157/162/166/162. Selected policy: GPT-5.6 Sol 100.00 RHAE (183 levels, 7,766 scored actions) and Opus 5 100.00 (6,641 actions).
cost: Opus 4.8 list-price totals about USD 5.66k (no model), 7.27k (single), 5.78k (orchestrator), 8.03k (trigger); GPT-5.6 Sol run USD 4.47k total (mean 179, median 114 per game, max 649); Opus 5 USD 2.99k total (mean 119, median 97 per game, max 303), per the paper's estimates. A USD 1.5k per-game ceiling nominally applied.
verified: arXiv API record + arXiv HTML full text (read relevant sections)
could_not_verify: The paper itself says end-of-run measurements cannot determine how earlier model versions affected action; one run per policy, no variance. Causal claim rests on 4 policies that differ in several ways at once. Cost figures are the paper's list-price estimates, not billed.

title: Twin: Playing an Unknown Game with a Test-Time Digital Twin
authors: Alexy Skoutnev, Kirill Acharya, Gaston Longhitano, et al.
mechanism: Per game, a frontier coding agent (OpenAI Codex, GPT-5.6 Sol, connected to the game only through files) starts from an identity-twin Python world model (T,R) and an empty log D of all observed transitions. Loop per move: Perceive the real grid; while Validate(T,D) returns gaps (twin fails to replay any logged transition), Explore ranks broken rules and Repair rewrites T (dynamics wall); then Plan by BFS inside the twin; if no plan, Explore ranks reachable candidates and ProposeGoal sets a tentative R (goal wall). Acceptance gates enforced by the harness: no scored action is issued until the twin reproduces every logged transition; a tentative goal must evaluate false on every logged frame; a candidate reached without a level boundary is never proposed again; actions are submitted under a halt-on-mismatch check, with each mismatch becoming a counterexample for repair.
evidence: ARC-AGI-3 public set (25 games, 183 levels). Twin scores 93.3, clears 23/25 games and 179/183 levels (97.8%), more efficiently than humans on 158 of 179 cleared levels; goal inferred before any reward on 156 of cleared levels (87.2%). Same base model played directly scores 7.8%; off-the-shelf Codex harness (no-twin ablation) 61.1 (13 games, 148 levels). Table 1: OPINE-World 78.4 (20 games, 160 levels), Prime Agent 78.3 with GPT-5.6 Sol (164 levels), EWM 63.8 with GPT-5.5 (14 games, 146 levels), Codex GPT-5.6 Sol 61.1. Twins predict 79% of first-seen state-action pairs exactly. 18 games reach 100.0.
cost: Twin used 2.60 billion processed tokens (47.8M non-cached) and 91.4 hours wall-clock inference across the 25 runs; roughly 224k tokens per scored action; per-game range 5.1M (sb26) to 625.3M (ka59) tokens; ka59 alone 24% of tokens. No-twin ablation: 1.06B tokens, 48k tok/action, 22,224 actions vs Twin 11,614 actions. EWM: 20.0B tokens, 715k tok/action. No dollar figure.
verified: arXiv API record + arXiv HTML full text (read relevant sections)
could_not_verify: No dollar cost, only tokens and hours; per-task cost expressed as tokens (224k/action; per-game 5.1M-625M). Not checked whether scores are single runs per game. Limitations stated: deterministic dynamics only, replay certifies only logged transitions, fixed search budgets, no long-temporal-context mechanics. Negative: Twin uses 2.4x total tokens and 4.7x tokens per action vs the no-twin ablation; tn36 (1.5x human) and ka59 (1.6x) need more actions than humans; OPINE-World ahead on g50t, sp80, sc25; two games not cleared. | code note: https://github.com/Alexyskoutnev/TWIN-ARC-AGI-3 (site: https://arc-agi-3-twin.vercel.app/)

title: NVIDIA-labs OO Agents: Native Python Object-Oriented Agents
authors: Paul Furgale, Severin Klingler, James Nolan, et al.
mechanism: NOOA is a general Python agent framework (agent = a Python class; methods with '...' bodies are completed by an LLM loop; CodeAct REPL; typed returns validated by the runtime; a memory subsystem attached via MemoryManager.install). For ARC-AGI-3 it runs one NOOA agent per game with a 50-line 'world-model skill': the agent persists an executable model as workspace modules (encode(grid)->z latent, predict(z,action)->z'), retrodicts every turn (a predict-vs-observed mismatch is stated to be 'the sole refinement signal'), searches over its own predict once trusted, and keeps memory across levels. Every turn ends with submit_actions(..., rationale='predict: ...'), so each action batch is a checked experiment. Acceptance gate for a model update: retrodiction mismatch is the refinement signal; the text read does not describe a separate held-out or hard-blocking acceptance check (unlike harness-enforced replay in Twin). It replaces DreamTeam's six role prompts (1,821 lines) and a 4,690-line harness-side retrodiction engine with framework primitives.
evidence: ARC-AGI-3 public 25 games, one agent per game, two-hour fleet cap: world-model skill + memory on GPT-5.5 RHAE 50.2% (118 levels) vs 41.7% baseline hypothesis-driven skill and 38.4% markdown-file memory ablation (+8.5 and +11.8 points); on GPT-5.6-sol 85.1% (170 levels). ARC Prize's own evaluation of raw GPT-5.6-sol averages 13.3% on the same 25 public games (paper: 6.4x harness effect; budgets differ so 'indicative'). 22 of 25 games persisted executable model code (~4.4k lines). Memory: 3,262 writes, 12,654 spontaneous injections, 27,115 deliberate reads at 99% hit rate; recalls/decision vs levels completed Spearman rho=+0.52. SWE-bench Verified GPT-5.5: 67.2% / 78.8% / 82.2% at off/high/xhigh vs OpenCode 78.6% and PI 78.2% at xhigh; Opus 4.6 79.8% vs 75.2%/75.8%. Terminal-Bench 2.0 GPT-5.5 off 46.1% (OpenCode 34.8, PI 37.1); high 73.0%; PI best at xhigh 75.3% vs NOOA 73.0%.
cost: ARC-AGI-3: guarded, cache-aware fleets cost $17.85 (GPT-5.5) and $13.28 (GPT-5.6-sol) per game at gpt-5.5 pricing; both fleets under $20 per game. Fleet cap two hours wall-clock. SWE-bench GPT-5.5 xhigh: ~28 model calls and ~1.1M tokens per task (OpenCode ~1.3M tokens, PI 66 calls and 2.2M tokens).
verified: arXiv API record + arXiv HTML full text (read relevant sections)
could_not_verify: No code URL. Strict acceptance gate for model updates not found (retrodiction is described as the signal; not verified whether code blocks actions on mismatch). Hardest-to-compare: 85.1% is on public games with a skill authored with access to them (not checked in text), and the 13.3% baseline uses a different evaluation budget. 85.1% phrased as 'is scoring' (live fleet), 'at the cap' for GPT-5.5 only. Not negative but notable: PI beats NOOA on Terminal-Bench 2.0 GPT-5.5 xhigh (75.3% vs 73.0%), and margins narrow at higher reasoning effort. | code note: No URL given for NOOA; text says BenchAgent is 'included in the NOOA repository'.

title: Continual Harness: Online Adaptation for Self-Improving Foundation Agents
authors: Seth Karten, Joel Zhang, Tersoo Upaa, et al.
mechanism: State is the harness H = (system prompt p, sub-agents G, skills K, memory M), starting from a minimal interface (frame, ASCII text map, buttons). The agent plays; every F steps after a warm-up of W steps a Refiner (same model as the agent) reads the recent trajectory window for failure signatures and runs four passes, one per component, applying CRUD edits through the same meta-tool API (define_agent, run_code, process_memory). The updated harness enters context on the next step; there is no reset, so refinement accumulates over the episode. No acceptance gate on harness edits is described: edits are applied directly (H_{t+1} = H_t (+) Delta). A second loop (co-learning) trains an open-source Gemma-4 model: K=256-step DAgger rollouts inside the live-refining harness, scored by a pairwise process reward model, low-reward windows relabelled by a Gemini-3.1-pro teacher, soft SFT update; emulator state carries over between iterations.
evidence: NOT ARC-AGI-3: environments are Pokemon Red and Emerald (metric: cumulative button presses to milestone; PokeAgent Challenge milestones, 31 for Emerald, 18 for Red). Text states Continual Harness 'substantially reduces button-press cost relative to the minimalist baseline and recovers a majority of the H_min-to-expert efficiency gap'. Emerald, Gemini 3 Pro: from-scratch CH reaches 100% of milestones at $130 median vs H_min at 98% for $215 (~40% cost reduction); bootstrap variants 96-100% at $110-$140. Flash: bootstrap-updating 80% at $42 vs H_min 77% for $30 (high variance). Flash-Lite: H_min 20% at $11; every CH variant falls to 3-13%. Gemma-4 co-learning: milestone index advances across iterations on five runs, untrained Gemma-4 baseline zero advance. GPP: completed Pokemon Blue, Yellow Legacy (hard mode), Crystal with human-in-the-loop refinement.
cost: Emerald 24-hour seeds; Gemini API spend reported per run (cached input at 25%): Pro CH $130 median vs H_min $215; Flash $42 vs $30; Flash-Lite ~$11. Co-learning: LoRA r=256 on H200 GPUs, 8K context; K=256 steps per iteration. Seeds: at least three.
verified: arXiv API record + arXiv HTML full text (read relevant sections)
could_not_verify: The task premise that this paper reports ARC-AGI-3 numbers is wrong: the string 'ARC-AGI' does not occur in the text; it is Pokemon only. No acceptance gate (validation, regression test, rollback) on Refiner edits was found. Website https://sethkarten.ai/continual-harness given, no code repository URL found. Total token counts not stated. Exact milestone numbers for Red are in figures, not text.

title: Workspace Optimization: How to Train Your Agent
authors: Elad Sarafian, Gal Kaplun, Ron Banner, et al.
mechanism: Frozen LLMs (no weight updates); the trainable state is the 'workspace': six typed surfaces each owned by one role (Observer: observation parser/render; Simulator: executable dynamics program predict()/history(); Inductive Explorer: sub-goals and policies; Transductive Explorer: probes; Critic: failure routing; Team Leader: action arbitration). Before each action the Simulator commits a one-step prediction as code; after the next observation the harness diffs predicted vs actual state, routes the diff component to the owning surface, and roles also send peer feedback; the owner patches its artifact. Gate: a regression set R_t (window of past transitions, rebuilt each step by replaying current programs against the stored trace) is run after every edit; transitions the previous version handled but the patch breaks become new counterexamples for the responsible role. Text says breakage 'informs the next round of edits' and the conclusion says repairs are 'replayed against earlier evidence before it is accepted'; no hard reject/rollback rule is spelled out in what I read.
evidence: ARC-AGI-3 25-game public set, official RHAE scorer, averaged over two independent runs: DreamTeam mean RHAE 38.36% vs Symbolica Agentica SDK single published run 36.08% (abstract: 36% to 38.4%). Environment actions: DreamTeam mean 444 per game vs Symbolica 16,081 (text calls this '31% reduction in mean per-game actions'; the arithmetic of 444 vs 16,081 does not read as 31%, unverified). Per solved level: 54.1 vs 100.1 actions (46% reduction); on 85 levels cleared by all, 49.0 vs 57.3 (-14.5%). On the 10 games unchanged by the April 14 benchmark update gap is +3.42 pp. Matched-budget human reference: DreamTeam ahead for first ~5 h, curves cross at ~5.3 h, human ahead through 24 h. Released frontier-LLM baselines cited: Gemini 3.1 Pro 0.37%, GPT-5.4 0.26%, Opus 4.6 0.25%, Grok 4.20 0%.
cost: Models: Observer/Simulator Claude Opus 4.6 (no reasoning); Team Leader/Transductive Explorer Opus 4.6 (low reasoning); Inductive Explorer/Critic GPT-5.5 (high reasoning). Per-step token budget 250,000; max 20 actions per step; 24-hour cap; Table 3 reports per-role LLM calls (~1.75-2.01 per env step), input K tokens (e.g. Observer 133.1K, Critic 154.1K) and output K tokens per step, pooled over 22,180 env steps. Paper says scores 'bounded by time and cost budgets'. No dollar figure found.
verified: arXiv API record + arXiv HTML full text (read relevant sections)
could_not_verify: No dollar cost. No ablations: Appendix E says 'Ablations, synthetic-game results, and game-family stratification are not claimed here'. Run 1 completed all 25 games; run 2 was operator-stopped with 18 games still in progress (partial RHAE used), so the 'two-run average' mixes a complete and a partial run. Only the single scorecard link (arcprize.org/scorecards/831c83cf-...) is public; Table 7 says single seed 0. No code repository for DreamTeam (only a reference to Symbolica's github.com/symbolica-ai/ARC-AGI-3-Agents). Whether a patch failing regression is hard-rejected not confirmed.

title: Graph-Based Exploration for ARC-AGI-3 Interactive Reasoning Tasks
authors: Evgenii Rudakov, Jonathan Shock, Benjamin Ultan Cowley
mechanism: Training-free, no LLM. A Frame Processor segments the 64x64 16-colour frame into single-colour connected components, masks probable status bars, assigns click candidates to five priority tiers (size, morphology, colour salience) and hashes the masked frame as a state id. A Level Graph Explorer keeps a directed graph of states and action transitions (per-action priority, tested status, successor, distance to nearest frontier). Hierarchical action selection: random untested action at priority <= p in the current state; else walk the shortest path to a reachable state with untested actions at priority <= p; else increment p. Deterministic games are assumed. There is no verification gate; the only signal is level completion.
evidence: ARC-AGI-3 Preview Challenge (6 games: public ft09, ls20, vc33; private sp80, lp85, as66; 8-10 levels each). Abstract: 'solves a median of 30 out of 52 levels across six games and ranks 3rd on the private leaderboard'. Full 8-hour run, median of 5 runs: 16 levels on private games and 14 on public games. With 4,000-interaction cap: 19 levels (2 ft09, 2 ls20, 5 vc33, 1 sp80, 2 lp85, 7 as66). Random agent solves 6 private levels (and 3 public); LLM+DSL (GPT-4.1) solves 5 private levels, i.e. below random. Official challenge evaluation: submitted model solved 12 levels on private games, ranking 3rd, due to a reset-handling bug.
cost: No LLM, so no token cost. Runs capped at 8 hours wall-clock at 10 steps per second shared across the three private games (max 96,000 steps per game). LLM+DSL baseline produced only about 4,000 interactions per game and was not re-run to avoid LLM cost.

title: WorldCoder, a Model-Based LLM Agent: Building World Models by Writing Code and Interacting with the Environment
authors: Hao Tang, Darren Key, Kevin Ellis
mechanism: WorldCoder keeps a replay buffer D of (s,a,r,s',c,d) tuples plus each episode's initial state and context, and a Python program (transition function T-hat, goal-conditioned reward function R-hat) as the world model over symbolic object-set states. Loop: act by planning in the current code model (planner is separate; MCTS used for AlfWorld), store the experience, and if the program fails a constraint, prompt GPT-4 with the erroneous program plus transitions it cannot explain (and, if needed, a random subset of D) to fix its code; repeat. Gate: a program is only accepted when it satisfies phi_1 (explains every stored transition and reward) AND phi_2 (optimism: given the initial state and goal, there exists an action sequence under the model reaching a positive-reward terminal state). Which program to refine next is chosen by REx (a bandit balancing refining promising vs rarely-refined programs) with heuristic h = fraction of replay buffer consistent with phi_1 plus (indicator phi_1) x fraction of (s0,c) pairs satisfying phi_2. Transfer across environments = refining an old program rather than writing a new one.
evidence: Sokoban: starting from only the goal 'win the game', the agent builds a world model over the first 50 actions; ReAct succeeds on only 15% +/- 8% of basic levels; deep RL (model-based and model-free) requires millions of experiences / >1 million steps for 2-box Sokoban (Fig 3D); cannot solve 5+ box levels (planner limitation). Optimism (phi_2) has little effect on Sokoban (dense reward). Minigrid: PPO needs 10^4-10^5 steps to learn valid policies in most environments and cannot solve UnlockPickup even in 3x10^8 steps; phi_2 is necessary for harder environments without transfer and for zero-shot new goals; 'prompt4reward' ablation struggles to follow new instructions. AlfWorld: synthesizes a 250+ line world model; optimism objective necessary for nonzero performance; typically solves the task in the first episode after about 20 exploratory steps. Abstract: more sample-efficient than deep RL, more compute-efficient than ReAct-style agents, transfers knowledge by editing code.
cost: 'after front-loading 400k LLM tokens (about $15), it can issue as many actions as needed without subsequent LLM queries' (Sokoban). Model: GPT-4 for refinement. Asymptotic LLM calls per new task O(1) vs O(T) for ReAct-style agents.

title: Generating Code World Models with Large Language Models Guided by Monte Carlo Tree Search
authors: Nicola Dainese, Matteo Merler, Minttu Alakuijala, et al.
mechanism: GIF-MCTS builds a Monte Carlo tree where nodes are partial programs (state = parent's code plus L=2 further lines; rollout = the remaining completion needed to run it) and edges are LLM actions. Selection uses UCT (with a custom exploration/exploitation heuristic, Appendix B); expansion calls the LLM with one of three actions; evaluation runs the rollout against unit tests (for a Code World Model, the fraction of transitions in 10 curated offline trajectories it predicts correctly) and the value is backpropagated. Three actions: (1) Generate new lines - LLM continues the node's code to a full program in a new branch; (2) Improve predictions - LLM is given the full parent program plus one wrongly predicted example (state, action, true next state, predicted next state) and asked for a chain-of-thought diagnosis and a rewrite; (3) Fix bugs - for programs that crash (reward 0) the LLM gets the error and fixes it; buggy nodes get a temporary value so UCT revisits them until fixed or attempts run out. Gate: program accuracy on the offline transitions (0 for non-executing code); search stops on matching all transitions or exhausting the LLM-call budget, best CWM returned.
evidence: CWMB (18 RL environments, discrete and continuous), Table 2, accuracy / normalized return R. Llama 3 70B (3 seeds, budget 50 LLM calls): GIF-MCTS discrete 0.84+/-0.03 acc, 0.76+/-0.03 R; continuous 0.35+/-0.03, 0.22+/-0.01. WorldCoder* (re-implementation): discrete 0.79+/-0.04, 0.60+/-0.04; continuous 0.32+/-0.03, 0.19+/-0.01. GPT-4 Turbo (1 seed, budget 10): GIF-MCTS discrete 0.91+/-0.08, 0.81+/-0.06; continuous 0.40+/-0.03, 0.26+/-0.01. WorldCoder* discrete 0.87+/-0.09, 0.79+/-0.06; continuous 0.24+/-0.06, 0.20+/-0.01. APPS competition split pass@20 (Llama 3 70B): GIF-MCTS 28.3+/-1.4, WorldCoder* 25.1+/-1.4, zero-shot CoT* 23.2+/-1.3. RTFM (simplified): GPT-4 Turbo budget 50 GIF-MCTS accuracy 1.00, R 1.00 vs WorldCoder* 0.64, R -0.06. Claim: planning with CWMs is 'from four to six orders of magnitude faster compared to directly querying an LLM as a world model'; only 10 trajectories of at most 100 steps used.
cost: Budget is counted in LLM calls: 50 for Llama 3 70B, 10 for GPT-4 Turbo on CWMB (extra GPT-4 Turbo runs at 50 only on RTFM, 'we couldn't do this on the full CWMB due to budget concerns'). No dollar or wall-clock figures for synthesis found in the text.

title: Code World Models for General Game Playing
authors: Wolfgang Lehrach, Daniel Hennes, Miguel Lazaro-Gredilla, et al.
mechanism: Before play, Gemini 2.5 Pro is given the game's natural-language rules plus 5 offline trajectories and writes a Python code world model (CWM) in OpenSpiel API format (state transition, legal moves, termination); for imperfect-information games it also writes an inference function (samples hidden state/history) and optionally a heuristic value function. Refinement: unit tests are auto-generated from every transition in the offline trajectories (states, observations, rewards, action legality, no execution errors); failing stack traces are fed back to the LLM. Two refinement modes: sequential conversation, or tree search a la REx with Thompson sampling over multiple CWMs (chosen for the rest of the paper). Refinement runs until transition accuracy is 1.0 or the LLM-call budget is exhausted. Value functions are not refined. For closed-deck (no hidden info) a 'CWM autoencoder' uses the inference function as encoder and the CWM as decoder. The CWM then drives (IS)MCTS (1,000 simulations).
evidence: 10 games: perfect-info Tic-tac-toe, Connect four, Backgammon, Generalized tic-tac-toe (OOD), Generalized chess (OOD); imperfect-info Leduc poker, Bargaining, Gin rummy, Quadranto (OOD), Hand of war (OOD). Abstract: 'our method outperforms or matches Gemini 2.5 Pro in 9 out of the 10 considered games.' Validation: held-out test set of 10,000 transitions from 100 games with random/MCTS players on ground-truth code, plus online transitions during play. CWM-MCTS ties GT-MCTS (ground-truth-code MCTS upper bound) and beats Gemini 2.5 Pro in all perfect-info games; CWM-ISMCTS beats or matches Gemini except Hand of war. Table 1 (open deck, tree search, hidden-history inference): Gin rummy transition accuracy train 0.7816 / test 0.7455 / online 0.9044, inference accuracy train 0.5857 / test 0.5376, 500.0 LLM calls; Hand of war inference test 0.9357; most others 1.0 train. Matches averaged over 100 games, CWM synthesis repeated 5 times with bad samples rejected.
cost: Synthesis model Gemini 2.5 Pro. Cost reported as number of LLM calls per game (Table 1: e.g. Leduc poker 4.4, Quadranto 6.0, Bargaining 23.0, Hand of war 338.2, Gin rummy 500.0 = budget). Tree search uses fewer calls than conversation. No dollars or tokens found.

title: Code as Worlds: Agentic Discovery of Executable World Representations for Physical Reasoning
authors: Hanyang Wang, Yimo Cai, Weiliang Chen, et al.
mechanism: NOT a game or agent-memory paper: it targets physical scenes. An Executable World Representation (EWR) p=(C,E,A) (physical composition, dynamic evolution, appearance) is expressed as code. From text or a real video (depth, SAM3 masks, tracks as evidence), an LLM agent runs a propose-instantiate-execute-render-verify loop for at most K rounds: instantiate as simulator parameters, run the simulator to a state trajectory, render to depth/masks/trajectories, compare predicted vs input evidence at key frames, aggregate discrepancies into structured feedback that guides local revision. The loop stops when the EWR explains the evidence parsimoniously; if the iteration budget is exhausted the hypothesis is rejected. Verified EWRs are then used to generate QA pairs with exact labels to train VLMs with SFT then GRPO.
evidence: Verification gate: yes, verifier-driven acceptance and rejection after K rounds (K=5 in the evaluation); results measured with metrics not included in the verification signal. At matched five-evaluation budget the loop beats Best-of-5 on Visual Alignment, Object IoU, Traj-ADE and Accuracy@2%D (numbers are in a figure). Application: QuantiPhy-validation, macro-average (MRA): Code-as-World-VL-4B 50.6, 9B 55.4, 27B (Reasoning) 58.6; proprietary: Gemini-3.1 Flash 54.8, ChatGPT-5.1 48.4, Gemini-2.5 Pro 46.4. Abstract: 'state-of-the-art performance on QuantiPhy and surpasses leading proprietary models'.
cost: Training of 4B and 9B variants on eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs, two-phase curriculum (SFT image-space grounding, then GRPO on executable-world VQA). Discovery-loop LLM, tokens and dollars not stated in what I read.

title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
authors: Noah Shinn, Federico Cassano, Edward Berman, et al.
mechanism: Three LLM roles: Actor (acts, conditioned on short-term memory = current trajectory and long-term memory = stored reflections), Evaluator (scores a trajectory), Self-Reflection model (turns the sparse reward/failure signal plus trajectory plus memory into a verbal summary sr_t). After each trial sr_t is appended to an episodic memory buffer mem, bounded by a sliding window of Omega experiences (usually 1-3); the Actor retries with the reflections in context. Loop runs until the Evaluator deems the trajectory correct (or trial cap / 3 consecutive failures in HotPotQA). Gate: none on the reflection text itself; the only gate is the Evaluator signal - environment reward/heuristic in ALFWorld (self-reflect when the agent repeats the same action >3 cycles or exceeds 30 actions), exact-match in HotPotQA, and self-generated unit tests (up to 6, AST-filtered) for code. No weights are updated.
evidence: Abstract: 91% pass@1 on HumanEval vs previous GPT-4 80%. Table 1 (pass@1): HumanEval Python 91.0 (prev SOTA 80.1 GPT-4), HumanEval Rust 68.0 (vs 60.0), MBPP Python 77.1 (vs 80.1 GPT-4, i.e. Reflexion is worse), MBPP Rust 75.4 (vs 70.9), Leetcode Hard Python 15.0 (vs 7.5). ALFWorld (134 tasks): improves over baselines by an absolute 22% in 12 iterative learning steps; ReAct + Reflexion completes 130 of 134 tasks. HotPotQA: improves by 20% (text); with ground-truth context CoT (GT) fails 39% of questions and Reflexion improves accuracy by 14%; self-reflection gives an 8% absolute boost over episodic-memory-only. title: AutoManual: Constructing Instruction Manuals by LLM Agents via Interactive Environmental Learning
authors: Minghao Chen, Yihang Li, Yanting Yang, et al.
mechanism: Two alternating online processes over a shared rule system Theta. (1) Planner (LLM) receives the rules, retrieved skill/reflection library items, task and observation, and writes free-form Python code as its plan; the episode is classed Direct Success / Indirect Success (errors then recovered) / Failure and the Planner writes a 'conclusion' (code block, mistakes summary, or failure reflection). (2) Builder reads the trajectory and manages rules via write_rule / update_rule / stop_generating. Rule format: Rule Type (one of Special Phenomenon, Special Mechanism, Useful Helper Method, Success Process, Corrected Error, Unsolved Error), Rule Content (starting with its scope), Example (code/remark from the trajectory), Validation Logs (episode and rule IDs tracing evolution). Case-conditioned prompting: Builder first classifies the main error as 'Imperfect Rules' or 'Imperfect Agent', then gets a targeted prompt to limit hallucinated rules (e.g. rules of success from a failed trajectory). Consolidator: when rule count exceeds N_max it merges/deletes related or redundant rules using get_trajectory, update_rule, delete_rule. Formulator then compiles rules into a human-readable manual used at test time. Gate: validation is by online re-use of rules in later episodes and environment feedback (no explicit held-out acceptance test); the Builder/Consolidator are LLM judgments.
evidence: ALFWorld test success (%), avg of 3 runs, 1 human example. GPT-3.5-turbo testing: AutoManual 86.2 (Put 95.8, Clean 79.6, Heat 87.0, Cool 78.8, Examine 100.0, Put two 66.7) vs Reflexion 59.8, ExpeL 52.2, AdaPlanner 63.3, Planner+Lib. 66.5, ReAct 41.9. GPT-4-turbo testing: AutoManual 97.4 vs Reflexion 85.9, Planner+Lib. 88.1, ExpeL 79.2, ReAct 76.8, AdaPlanner 76.4. MiniWoB++ (all 53 types, 4 examples): GPT-3.5 AutoManual 92.7 vs AdaPlanner 89.4, RCI 77.3; GPT-4-turbo AutoManual 98.3 vs AdaPlanner 90.3, RCI 88.6. MiniWoB++ 9 types with feedback (1 example): GPT-3.5 82.2 vs AdaPlanner 71.6; GPT-4-turbo 94.5 vs AdaPlanner 74.1, Planner+Lib. 80.2. WebArena (Reddit): AutoManual 65.1 vs SteP 55.0, AutoGuide 43.7, Planner 51.1, ReAct 6.0. Ablations (ALFWorld GPT-4-turbo): offline rule management 88.1 -> 90.7 only; no skill & reflection libraries 97.4 -> 89.5; no case-conditioned prompts 93.8 -> 97.4 with them.

title: WALL-E: World Alignment by Rule Learning Improves World Model-based LLM Agents
authors: Siyu Zhou, Tianyi Zhou, Yijun Yang, et al.
mechanism: World model = frozen LLM + a learned rule set (natural-language rules R^NL plus code rules R^code). Each iteration the agent (MPC, look-ahead planning with the world model) collects a real trajectory; predicted transitions are compared to real ones on the binary action_result and split into correct / incorrect sets. An LLM induces new NL rules from real trajectories (distinct from previous rules), then refines existing rules (modifies/discards conflicting ones), then translates NL rules to code. Gate: code rules are executed against the labeled predicted transitions and any rule that fails to predict a transition correctly is discarded; the survivors are pruned by a greedy maximum-coverage selection over the transitions the bare LLM got wrong (rules covering only correct transitions or fully redundant are dropped, and dropped code rules are also removed from the NL set). At inference NL rules go in the prompt; code rules override the LLM prediction as a verification layer (ApplyRules). Gradient-free.
evidence: Minecraft (Table 1, success rate %, avg): WALL-E 69 (15.77 replanning rounds) vs GITM 54 (25.49), DEPS 37 (35.36), WALL-E w/o WM 61 (23.13), Optimus-1* 47, Jarvis-1* 42, Human 59. Per level WALL-E: Wooden 98, Stone 91, Iron 63, Golden 69, Diamond 46, Redstone 48. ALFWorld (Table 3, 134 test tasks, avg): WALL-E 95; RAFA 95; AdaPlanner 91; Reflexion 86; ReAct 74; EMMA 82; Human 91. Abstract: 'In Minecraft, WALL-E exceeds baselines by 15-30% in success rate while costing 8-20 fewer replanning rounds and only 60-80% of tokens. In ALFWorld, its success rate surges to a new record high of 95% only after 6 iterations.' Ablation (Table 4): LLM agent + LLM world model 38(33.53); rules in world model 69(15.77); rules in agent only 61(23.13); rules in both 67(16.59). World model without rules barely helps. Rule set stops changing after 4 iterations.
cost: Table 2 Minecraft avg tokens (USD): WALL-E 60348.71 (0.41), GITM 74638.54 (0.51), DEPS 93560.95 (0.65), WALL-E w/o WM 72390.16 (0.52). title: Belief-Calibrated Optimization: An Explicit World Model for Agentic Optimization
authors: Yuhan Chen, Zhihua Tian, Mahavir Dabas, et al.
mechanism: A coding-agent proposer edits an agent scaffold iteratively. BCO adds one persistent Markdown document world_model_calibration.md (the 'world model'), a set of atomic beliefs each = (falsifiable claim, applicability conditions, confidence in [0,1], status hypothesis/confirmed/refuted, supporting and contradicting evidence, 'mass' = approx. number of observed failures explained) plus an Experiments section and an append-only History. Each iteration the proposer writes prediction.md (belief at stake, edit mechanism, claim about a task subset) BEFORE any source change, evaluates the candidate, then at the start of the next iteration grades the prediction against per-task results and traces and applies Add/Revise/Merge/Remove operations to the beliefs one at a time. Acceptance rule: there is no explicit accept/reject gate on beliefs or edits; the proposer itself grades and edits the document, and the final scaffold is the evaluated candidate with the highest train passrate (top-1 train-frontier, ties to earliest iteration; best-of-three on the two memory benchmarks). The document starts empty; pre-seeding guessed failure modes is forbidden. 'vanilla' control = same loop with the calibration include removed.
evidence: Table 1 (train / held-out passrate, vanilla vs bco; initial): LME train 0.160 initial, 0.590 vanilla, 0.710 bco; held-out 0.148 / 0.533 / 0.608. LoCoMo train 0.288/0.412/0.475; held-out 0.295/0.375/0.453. GAIA train 0.400/0.425/0.575; held-out 0.283/0.343/0.495. AppWorld train 0.600/0.800/0.933; held-out 0.694/0.766/0.796. TB2.0 train 0.450/0.525/0.550; held-out 0.477/0.470/0.492. Text: bco higher on train by +0.025 (TB2.0) to +0.150 (GAIA); held-out +0.022 (TB2.0) to +0.152 (GAIA). Offline ablation on 40 candidates (None/Scrambled/Intact): upside hit rate 0.441/0.460/0.538; downside precision 0.142/0.181/0.217; sign-test p=0.125 over 4 runs. Persistence-without-calibration on LongMemEval-s, 3 trajectories x 10 iterations: vanilla 0.430, Notes 0.427, bco 0.467.
